worksheet.title: The Wrong Block Inside
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find and fix a wrong block inside a loop.

parts.title: Right count, wrong block
text: Sometimes the repeat number is correct, but a BLOCK inside the loop is wrong. The loop runs the right number of times — it just does the wrong action.
Read what Bit should do, then find the inside block that does not match.

parts.title: Bit should clap then STOMP — but this is buggy
parts.note: The repeat 3 is right, but the second block should be STOMP, not clap. Fix the second block.

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: Bit should do clap, stomp — but the loop has clap, clap. Which block is wrong, and what should it be?

parts.title: Fix the turtle
parts.prompt: This should draw a SQUARE:  for i in range(4): bit.forward(50); bit.forward(50). But Bit draws a straight line! Which inside block is wrong, and what should it be?

parts.title: Write the fix
parts.prompt: Bit should do jump, spin, but the loop has jump, jump. Write the block that the SECOND one should be: ______

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: The square code  for i in range(4): bit.forward(50); bit.forward(50)  makes Bit go forward 8 times in a line. WHY is it a line and not a square? What block is missing?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A loop can repeat the right number of times but still be wrong if a block INSIDE is wrong. Check that every inside block matches what Bit should do.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students find a loop where the repeat number is right but a block INSIDE is wrong — in block and shape cases — and describe how the wrong block changes the result (a square becomes a straight line). The method here is SHOULD → DOES → FIX: say what the code SHOULD do, run it to see what it DOES, then FIX the one thing that is wrong. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the code and what Bit should do. Optional: a Scratch-style app (for the block loops) or a free Python-turtle playground (for the shapes) to run the code — you only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). The repeat number is right, but an inside block is wrong, so the result is wrong.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — the second block should be stomp, not clap.
3. Let them work. Students fix a square drawn as a line (Ex 2–3) and explain why two forwards with no turn make a line (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — the second block is wrong; change clap to stomp. Exercise 2 — the second "move forward" is wrong; change it to "turn right 90".
Exercise 3 — spin. Exercise 4 (challenge) — with two forwards and no turn, Bit just keeps going straight (8 forwards in a line); the turn block is missing.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing the repeat number. Here the count is right; an inside block is wrong.
Make it easier: compare the goal pattern to the blocks inside, one at a time.
Make it harder: ask which inside block makes a square versus a line.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, find what is wrong, fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child keeps the repeat number and fixes the wrong inside block.
